history.heading: Ancient cultures and the Incas
paragraphs: Ecuador was home to some of the earliest cultures of the Americas, such as the Valdivia culture on the coast, which made pottery around 3500 BCE. Later peoples included the Cañari and the Kingdom of Quito. The Inca Empire conquered the region in the late 15th century, and Quito became a northern Inca capital.

Spanish conquistadors arrived in the 1530s, during a civil war between the Inca brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar. Quito, refounded in 1534, became the seat of the Royal Audiencia of Quito, and its colonial centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: Independence and the republic
paragraphs: Quito proclaimed one of the first calls for independence in Latin America in 1809. Independence was secured in 1822 at the Battle of Pichincha, and Ecuador was part of Gran Colombia until 1830.

The republic was marked by rivalry between conservative Quito and liberal, commercial Guayaquil. Eloy Alfaro's Liberal Revolution of 1895 separated church and state. Ecuador lost territory to Peru in a 1941 war, and a final border agreement was signed in 1998.

history.heading: Modern Ecuador
paragraphs: Oil was discovered in the Amazon in the 1960s, transforming the economy. Political instability in the 1990s and 2000s saw several presidents removed, and after a banking crisis Ecuador adopted the US dollar in 2000. Rafael Correa governed from 2007 to 2017.
Since around 2020, violence by drug-trafficking gangs has surged. In 2024 the government declared an "internal armed conflict" against gangs after armed men stormed a television studio.

culture.heading: Peoples and languages
paragraphs: Most Ecuadorians are mestizo, with large indigenous communities, mainly Kichwa-speaking, and Afro-Ecuadorians, especially in Esmeraldas. Spanish is the official language, and Kichwa and Shuar are official languages of intercultural relations. Most people are Catholic.
The Panama hat is actually made in Ecuador from toquilla straw, a craft recognised by UNESCO. The Otavalo market is famous for indigenous textiles.

culture.heading: Food and nature
paragraphs: Popular dishes include ceviche, locro de papa (potato soup), encebollado (fish soup) and cuy (guinea pig) in the highlands. Ecuador is a top producer of fine cacao.
The Galápagos Islands, whose unique wildlife inspired Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, belong to Ecuador. Ecuador's 2008 constitution was the first in the world to recognise rights of nature.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Ecuador is a presidential republic with a unicameral National Assembly. Presidents serve four-year terms. Daniel Noboa was elected in 2023 and re-elected in 2025, prioritising a hard line against organised crime.
Indigenous movements, led by CONAIE, are a powerful political force and have organised major protests over fuel prices and mining.

economy.heading: Oil, bananas and shrimp
paragraphs: Ecuador is the world's largest exporter of bananas and a leading exporter of shrimp. Oil remains a major export and source of government revenue; in 2023 voters chose to halt oil drilling in part of Yasuní National Park. Cacao, flowers, and tourism, especially to the Galápagos, are also important.

Ecuador has used the US dollar as its currency since 2000, which brought price stability but limits economic policy. Insecurity, energy shortages caused by droughts affecting hydropower, and public debt are major challenges.
